statement.before: Cut a masonry arch along any joint. The part on one side of the cut is held in equilibrium by its support, its own weight and the loads on it, and by the force that the other part exerts across the joint. That force has a magnitude, a direction and a line of action, and it crosses the joint at a single point. The **line of thrust** is the locus of these crossing points over all the joints: a polygon, in the limit of ever thinner voussoirs a curve. It is the funicular polygon of the loads on the arch, and it marks the path along which the compressive force runs through the stone. If it crosses a joint of depth $t$ at distance $e$ from the middle, the whole joint is in compression while $|e| \le t/6$ (the middle third); for $t/6 < |e| \le t/2$ part of the joint is open (cracked); beyond $t/2$ the line has left the stone and the joint cannot carry the force.
statement.after: Cut a masonry arch along any joint. The part on one side of the cut is held in equilibrium by its support, its own weight and the loads on it, and by the force that the other part exerts across the joint. That force has a magnitude, a direction and a line of action, and it crosses the joint at a single point. The **line of thrust** is the locus of these crossing points over all the joints: a polygon, in the limit of ever thinner voussoirs a curve. It is the funicular polygon of the loads on the arch, and it marks the path along which the compressive force runs through the stone. For a rectangular joint of depth $t$, a full-contact linear elastic pressure profile stays compressive while $|e|\le t/6$ (the middle third). In its no-tension triangular-contact continuation, $t/6<|e|<t/2$ gives partial contact. These stress assumptions are additional to a no-tension resultant test: arbitrary nonnegative pressure need not be linear or determine the same contact region. A resultant beyond $|e|=t/2$ cannot be carried without tension; equality at an edge with positive force is an unlimited-pressure limiting hinge, not a finite pressure field.

scope.before: Plane arch with radial joints under self-weight; units are a half-span of 1 and a unit weight of 22 kN/m³ per metre of depth.
scope.after: Plane arch with radial joints under self-weight; units are a half-span of 1 and a unit weight of 22 kN/m³ per metre of depth. The middle-third and triangular partial-contact descriptions assume the stated rectangular, linear-elastic/no-tension stress model; they do not identify an arbitrary joint's actual cracking.

statement.before: Take a masonry structure that obeys Heyman’s assumptions (arch-3.4) under given loads. If a line of thrust can be found that is in equilibrium with the loads and lies everywhere inside the masonry, the structure is **safe**: it will not collapse under those loads. The line need not be the one that actually acts, and need not be unique; its existence is enough, and one can search for it with any trial thrust. If no such line exists, safety can no longer be shown and the structure can collapse by forming hinges (arch-3.6). For an arch the admissible lines form a convex family, so the horizontal thrust that goes with them lies in an interval $[H_{\min}, H_{\max}]$ that shrinks to a point when the arch is at the limit of safety.
statement.after: Take a masonry structure that obeys Heyman’s assumptions (arch-3.4) under given loads. If a line of thrust can be found that is in equilibrium with the loads and lies everywhere inside the masonry, the structure is **safe**: it will not collapse under those loads. The line need not be the one that actually acts, and need not be unique; its existence is enough, and one can search for it with any trial thrust. If no such line exists, safety can no longer be shown and the structure can collapse by forming hinges (arch-3.6). For an arch the admissible lines form a convex family, so the horizontal thrust that goes with them lies in an interval $[H_{\min}, H_{\max}]$ which can shrink to a point in a nondegenerate limiting case. A limiting feasible set can also contain several reaction states; a unique thrust is not guaranteed by convexity alone.

idea.before:
This is the lower-bound (static) theorem of plastic theory (solid-4.10) for a material with no tensile strength and unlimited compressive strength: a state of equilibrium that violates no yield condition certifies safety, whatever the real state of the structure is. One does not need to know how the real arch is cracked, or how far its supports have moved, only that cracks and small movements let it find some admissible state. For the arch the three unknown reactions $(H, V_0, m_0)$ make every condition "the line crosses joint $j$ inside the stone" a linear inequality, so the admissible lines are a polytope whose extreme thrusts are found by a small linear program. Poleni's argument for the dome of St Peter's, and Hooke's inversion (arch-3.1), both use the idea in this form.

The static-certificate argument uses the actual lower-bound proof of solid 4.10, not its particular plastic-beam formula. Here its ideal contact specialization is compression-only unilateral contact with no sliding: a closed contact has zero relative normal velocity, an opening contact carries zero normal force, and tangential relative motion is excluded. These are the workless contact/normal-cone conditions behind the ideal dissipation argument. Equilibrium and admissibility are checked for the present fixed geometry and supports; changing that geometry requires a new certificate. Neither convex inequalities alone nor an arbitrary elastic stress guess proves the material/contact hypotheses, and finite crushing, sliding or geometric instability lies outside this certificate.
